title: Nitroduck Wants to Make Gene Editing Accessible to Every Crop Breeder
summary: Nitroduck Wants to Make Gene Editing Accessible to Every Crop Breeder
body_markdown:
The hard part of improving a crop isn't deciding which trait to change. It's that developing a new variety still depends largely on chance: cross two parents, raise thousands of seedlings, wait years to see how each grows, looks, and tastes, and hope one is worth moving forward. For fruits, vegetables, and nuts, that process can take eight to sixteen years.


Gene editing was supposed to turn that lottery into a decision. In staple crops, it has made significant progress. But for much of the produce aisle, the technology remains out of reach.


Traditional CRISPR methods require delivering gene-editing machinery into an isolated plant cell, then regenerating that cell into an entire plant. This tissue-culture process must be developed separately for individual varieties, often requiring years of laboratory work and potentially millions of dollars.


As a result, gene editing remains inaccessible for roughly 85% of crops, according to Nitroduck. Around 80% of plant gene-editing research focuses on staple crops, leaving breeders of fruits, vegetables, and nuts with few practical alternatives to conventional crossing.


**Nitroduck, a Y Combinator Fall 2026 startup, is building a way around that bottleneck by delivering CRISPR through pollen.**


Instead of editing isolated plant cells and regenerating entire plants in a sterile laboratory, Nitroduck's approach introduces gene-editing machinery into pollen grains. The treated pollen then fertilizes a flower, allowing the edit to be incorporated into the resulting seed.


The approach builds on a workflow breeders already use. Pollen is routinely collected, stored, shipped, and exchanged across breeding programs. By integrating gene editing into that existing process, Nitroduck aims to make precision breeding accessible without requiring customers to establish their own molecular biology laboratories or tissue-culture facilities.


The technology is still in development, but the potential implications extend well beyond simplifying a laboratory procedure.


## From iGEM Champions to Y Combinator Founders


Nitroduck was founded by **Matej Zámečník, Matúš Grieš, and Miroslav Rosputinský** , three researchers who have spent the past six years developing new approaches to plant genetic engineering.


Together, they founded and led the Brno team that won the **Overgraduate Grand Prize at the 2025 iGEM synthetic biology competition** , competing against more than 330 teams from around the world, including teams from Ivy League universities.


Their award-winning work enabled gene editing in duckweed, one of the world's fastest-growing plants. According to the founders, their collective experience includes engineering four times as many plants as the average plant scientist does over an entire career.


Now, as part of Y Combinator's Fall 2026 batch, they're applying that experience to making gene editing accessible to breeders of fruits, vegetables, and nuts.


## A Gene-Editing Service Built Around Breeders


Nitroduck's proposed business model is designed to fit directly into existing breeding operations.


A breeder would ship pollen to Nitroduck along with a requested genetic trait. Nitroduck would edit the pollen and return it to the breeder, who could then use it in their own breeding program.


The breeder wouldn't need to purchase specialized laboratory equipment, obtain a CRISPR license, or hire a molecular biology team. Nitroduck also wouldn't need to grow the resulting plants, avoiding one of the most expensive and time-consuming parts of crop development.


Cost is another critical part of the company's strategy.


Today's gene-editing arrangements can involve substantial upfront fees and ongoing royalties on commercial sales. For breeders operating in markets where growers are highly sensitive to seed prices, those costs can make even valuable improvements financially impractical.


Nitroduck aims to replace that structure with affordable, flat-fee editing services.


The goal is to make gene editing economical for a much broader range of improvements, including flavor, color, texture, disease resistance, and other traits that influence what consumers buy.


## The Long-Term Opportunity: Crops That Keep Up With Disease


One of Nitroduck's longer-term ambitions is reducing agriculture's reliance on pesticides.


Plant pathogens continually evolve, often overcoming genetic resistance faster than breeders can develop and commercialize replacement varieties. When resistance breaks down, growers frequently turn to chemical treatments to protect their crops.


If breeders could introduce new resistance traits quickly and affordably, they could respond to emerging pathogens without restarting a conventional breeding process that might take another decade.


That could make gene editing a repeatable tool for crop protection rather than an expensive, one-time intervention.


For now, Nitroduck's immediate milestone is more focused: **producing edited seeds from treated pollen in a commercially relevant specialty crop, within an existing breeder's program.**


Achieving that would demonstrate a new path toward making precision gene editing available to the crops, breeders, and consumers that have largely been left out of the technology's advances.
